data.headword: mšaḥalle/mšaḥən; mašḥalle/mašḥən qarʕe d-u=səsyo 'ein Pferd warmreiten, zum Losstürmen bringen'
data.turoyo: Əmmi, Genǧ Xalil Aġa rawəx ʕal u səsyayḏe, mašḥalle qarʕe du səsyo w maflatle qarʕe du səsyo b ġar d əzzele l Ḥasane Aliki, d qoṭele.
data.translation: Da bestieg Gendsch Chalil Agha sein Pferd, machte ihm den Kopf warm und ließ es los galoppieren, um auf Ḥasan Aliki loszustürmen und ihn zu töten.

rationale: Repeated equestrian collocation in II and III. The explicit horse-head object followed by releasing the horse for a charge supports the construction. Permitted searches find an existing III quotation, but no separately listed idiom; add the idiom here without duplicating or moving that existing example.

summary: I distinguishes nominal temperature subjects from impersonal clauses with l-experiencers (26/172; 91/40; MAC MuA 19/30). The l-suffix in II may instead be a patient or a beneficiary (MAC NE Dilo and Falako/60-61); roles must be resolved from syntax.

Cooking procedures repeatedly juxtapose II causative heating, I attained heat in Preterit Intransitive, and I Part act. states (JTM 1.1/74,84). Infectum-wa gives recurrent past processing; bare Infectum may occur inside it (JL 11.12/3). No general tense reformulation is needed.
Both II and III have warming uses. Preserve mšaḥ- versus mašḥ- in the editions; 29/155 has conflicting collateral quotations, so this sample does not establish a dialect boundary.

The Detransitive evidence is small: one distinct MAC verse with repeated finite gmišaḥno and one JTM result-state mšaḥne. These show agent omission and patient-state focus, not a separate heating technique.

Bundled references under a quoted example can cite parallel attestations with different participants. 78/58 therefore remains in the existing heating reference bundle even though its object is a sword tip, not a seal.
Does cannon mšaḥalle at topat in PrS 19/34 specify priming, firing, or actual heating? The translation compresses mšaḥalle and mḥele arbʕo and cannot decide the lexical action.
Does šaḥini in 63/104 mean fermentation itself, rather than warming as part of wine-making?
Confirm the exact riding practice denoted by warming a horse or its head; the contexts establish preparation for a charge but not whether warming is literal in every instance.
Check the source alternation mašḥalle/mšaḥalle in 29/155 and whether the new III Infectum attestation reflects an independent stem or a dialect variant.

Literal heating covers milk, butter, ovens, vessels, baths, stones and sun-heated wine. No participant-based proliferation of senses; Part act. expresses warm/hot states already represented in the entry.
63/104 places šaḥini of grape juice in a fifteen-day transition to wine. A lexical meaning 'gären' remains unproven; literal warming and fermentation can coincide.
